newsitem.title: USA: Gold prices sink on Holocaust compensation plan.
newsitem.headline: Gold prices sink on Holocaust compensation plan.

text.p: Gold prices fell sharply Wednesday following news of a Swiss plan to set up a fund to compensate victims of the Holocaust to be financed by selling Swiss gold reserves.
"The Swiss news was only significant because it again says European central banks are now prepared to sell gold," CPM Group analyst Ted Kempf said.

The Swiss government proposed a fund to compensate victims of the Holocaust, financed by the sale of about 40 metric tons of gold a year over 10 years from the Swiss National Bank's reserves of about 2,583 tons.
Gold's rally of the past month had already been losing steam, traders said.
"The Swiss news was just the straw that broke the camel's back," FIMAT New York trader John Tyree said.
April gold fell $6.10 to $354.50 an ounce at New York's Commodity Exchange after earlier dropping as low as $352.50.
Coffee prices on New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, in contrast, continued to soar, racing to their highest level since October 1994 and sailing through the widely watched $2 a pound mark.
In yet another hectic session, roaster buying sent prices sharply higher from the opening bell. Speculators joined the buying spree, driving the benchmark May contract up 14.25 cents at one point.

"There is a lack of sellers because everyone who wanted to sell the market already sold it," said Victor Henriquez, managing director of Hencorp Becstone, a coffee trading firm in Miami. "As long as there is no coffee coming into the market, no one can stop it," he said of the rally.
Recent news of supply disruptions in Colombia and Central America have helped drive prices higher, while forecasts for a bigger Brazilian harvest have done little to slow the rally.
"This is the epitomy of a bull market. Whatever news comes out it's going to be regarded as bullish news," one London based coffee trader said.
A bullish price forecast issued earlier this week by Merrill Lynch has also contributed to recent strong gains.
"The prediction by Merrill Lynch that coffee is going to $3 made everybody and his grandmother buy the market," one New York trader said, referring to comments on Tuesday by analyst Judith Ganes.
May coffee rose 5.40 cents to $2.65 cents a pound after hitting $2.095 cents, the highest level since October 1994.
Crude oil futures slipped as the market failed to take heart from a drop in the nation's inventories last week.
But gasoline futures edged higher amid worries that a strike in Brazil might spread and threaten some U.S. imports.
Benchmark light crude futures for April delivery hit a high of $20.89 a barrel during the regular session but slipped back to $20.49, down 17 cents on the day.
"Basically, the market said it didnt believe the numbers on crude," said Ed Kevelson, a trader at Paribas Futures in New York, referring to data showing a drop in crude stocks last week.
The American Petroleum Institute late on Tuesday and the Energy Information Agency on Wednesday morning reported draws on crude stocks last week of 7.6 million and 5.4 million barrels, respectively.
Gasoline stocks fell 1.3 million barrels last week.
"The market is trying to establish some sort of base and I think it could do that here, possibly off the gasoline," said Steve Platt, an analyst at Dean Witter in Chicago.
April gasoline rose 0.44 cent to 63.33 cents a gallon.
